results.quantity: Relative plasma valine level, MCI vs cognitively normal older controls, cross-sectional. Both papers report this quantity for plasma, and both report it as lower in MCI. The candidate's 'increase' for P-1220 comes from the abstract and conclusion ('valine increased progressively (controls < MCI < AD)'). That claim merges biofluids: in P-1220 the MCI-vs-control rise is in urine, the AD-vs-MCI rise is in saliva, and the plasma MCI-vs-control result is a decrease.
results.finding_a: P-1396 (Meng et al. 2024, Front Aging Neurosci; 124 MCI (MoCA < 26) and 47 controls from 17 rural villages in Jimo District, Qingdao; 12-h fasting plasma; targeted UHPLC-QTRAP MS/MS (H650 panel, MRM, internal standards, sum-normalised)). Table 3, p.7 (multivariate criteria VIP > 1 and FDR < 0.05): Valine, MCI/CON FC 0.90, VIP 2.34, direction down, FDR < 0.01. Valine is not among the 11 univariate differential metabolites in Table 2 (p.6), because FC 0.90 does not pass the FC < 0.67 cut-off. The Discussion (p.9) confirms that leucine, isoleucine and valine were 'significantly decreased in the MCI group'. One sentence contradicts this internally: section 3.3 (p.4) says the heatmap showed valine and other essential amino acids 'significantly increased in the MCI group'. Table 3, the text just before it ('Except for cystine and argininosuccinic acid, the remaining amino acids were significantly decreased') and the Discussion all give a decrease, so that sentence is a slip.
results.finding_b: P-1220 (Cadaxo et al. 2026, Brain Research; 16 MCI, 30 LOAD and 48 controls aged 65+, comorbidity-free, ethnically mixed, recruited from UERJ clinics in Rio de Janeiro; non-fasting; 1H NMR CPMG on plasma, urine and saliva; Pareto-scaled binned spectra; Mann-Whitney U with BKY FDR). PLASMA, p.3: 'In MCI vs. controls, ... glucose, creatinine, creatine, asparagine, choline, leucine, valine, citrate, histidine, pyruvate, N-acetylglycoproteins, acetate and alanine were reduced (Fig. 1).' URINE, p.5: 'In MCI vs. controls comparison, valine and citrate were elevated.' SALIVA, p.6: 'Compared with MCI, AD showed slightly higher valine and alanine.' The paper's own Discussion (p.8) states the split directly: 'citrate and valine were lower in plasma and higher in urine.' No per-metabolite p-value or fold change appears in the main text; the statistics are in Supplementary Table 1, and significance vs control is marked by asterisks in Fig. 1.
results.same_quantity: Compared plasma to plasma, the two results are close to the same quantity, and they agree. Marker: valine in both. Fluid: plasma in both, but only when P-1220's plasma result is used; the abstract claim the miner used is not a plasma result. Assay: differs. P-1396 uses targeted MS with internal standards and sum normalisation; P-1220 uses NMR binned spectra with Pareto scaling and no absolute concentrations (its limitations, p.11). Sampling: P-1396 fasting 12 h; P-1220 non-fasting (p.2). Contrast: MCI vs cognitively normal controls in both, cross-sectional. Population: both are older adults. P-1396 defines MCI by MoCA screening (< 26, +1 for education) in a rural community sample. P-1220 uses clinician diagnosis (Albert 2011 criteria) and excludes people with comorbidities. Metric: the direction of the group difference, with FDR-controlled significance. The candidate's pairing compared P-1396's plasma decrease with P-1220's urine increase, or with an ordering that merges fluids. Plasma and urine valine are different quantities: urinary excretion is not circulating level. That pairing, taken literally, would be documented incommensurability. The correct plasma pairing is concordant.
results.incompatible: No. In plasma both studies report valine lower in MCI than in controls. P-1396 reports FC 0.90 at FDR < 0.01 (Table 3, p.7). P-1220 lists valine among the metabolites reduced in MCI vs controls (p.3), and its Discussion (p.8) restates 'valine ... lower in plasma'. Same direction, both significant, so there is no disagreement. The opposite direction exists only against P-1220's urine result, and against its abstract and conclusion, which merge the urine MCI>control rise and the saliva AD>MCI rise into 'controls < MCI < AD'. Neither is a plasma result. The candidate claim therefore misstates P-1220 for the plasma quantity.

results.quantity: Pooled standardized mean difference (SMD) of blood NfL between clinical MCI and cognitively healthy controls, cross-sectional, random effects. P-1275 pools 48 blood cohorts across all assays and both serum and plasma. P-1341 has no single blood pool. It reports plasma (2 studies), serum (1 study) and a Simoa subgroup, which holds exactly the same 3 blood studies and so is its de facto blood pool.
results.finding_a: P-1275 (Gaur et al. 2023, Ageing Res Rev 91:102046). Blood NfL: 48 study cohorts, 6517 MCI / 9438 controls, SMD 0.41 [0.32, 0.49], Z = 9.33, p < 0.001, I2 = 80.04% (Table 1, p.3; forest plot Fig. 3, p.6). After trim-and-fill: 0.36 [0.27, 0.45] (p.3). CSF NfL: 0.69 [0.56, 0.83]. Blood NfL is smaller than CSF NfL, but raised.
results.finding_b: P-1341 (Zhang et al. 2022, Medicine 101:e28932). Overall, across 7 studies (676 MCI / 504 HC): SMD 0.36 [0.04, 0.68], P = .03 (p.3). CSF (4 comparisons): 0.61 [0.21, 1.01], P < .01. Plasma (2 comparisons: Thijssen 2020 -0.15 [-0.52, 0.22] and Lin 2018 0.32 [0.02, 0.62]): 0.10 [-0.36, 0.56], I2 = 73%, P = .67 (text p.3; Fig. 3 p.4). Serum (1 study, Steinacker 2018): -0.33 [-1.03, 0.37], P = .36 (Fig. 3 p.4). Simoa (the same 3 blood studies): 0.01 [-0.38, 0.41], I2 = 62%, P = .95 (p.4; Fig. 5 p.5). The authors conclude that blood NfL 'may be not a biomarker of MCI in our study and more studies on blood NfL are needed' (p.5).
results.same_quantity: Broadly yes. Marker: NfL in both. Fluid: blood in both, serum and plasma. Contrast: MCI vs cognitively healthy controls, cross-sectional, in both. Metric: random-effects SMD in both. Population class: clinical MCI in older adults in both. P-1275 excludes MCI due to other neurological disorders such as PD. P-1341 requires 'adequate' MCI definitions and controls free of confounding disease. There is no adjustment set in either. Two differences remain. First, P-1341's blood evidence is Simoa-only and just 3 studies (147 MCI / 174 HC), while P-1275 pools all assays across 48 cohorts. Second, P-1341 never pools blood as one subgroup: it splits plasma and serum. Neither difference changes what is estimated enough to fail the same-quantity element. The pair fails on incompatibility, not on quantity.
results.incompatible: No. This is a difference in significance only, and the intervals overlap. P-1275's blood-NfL CI [0.32, 0.49] lies entirely inside P-1341's plasma CI [-0.36, 0.56]. P-1341's Simoa/all-blood CI [-0.38, 0.41] covers 0.32 to 0.41, the lower part of P-1275's interval. So neither estimate's uncertainty excludes the other. P-1341's plasma point estimate (0.10) is positive, the same direction as P-1275. The only negative point estimate is the single serum study, n = 32, whose CI [-1.03, 0.37] is not significant and does not exclude P-1275's estimate either. P-1341's conclusion that blood NfL was not confirmed is a failure to reach significance in a 2-3 study subgroup. It is not evidence of no difference, so the two opposite-sounding conclusions are both compatible with a small positive blood-NfL SMD. The evidence is also nested: all three P-1341 blood studies appear in P-1275's blood forest plot. Lin et al. 2018 and Steinacker et al. 2018 appear under the same names. The Thijssen study appears as 2020 in P-1341 and as 2021 in P-1275, with different estimates (-0.15 vs -0.04), so it may be a different report on an overlapping cohort. P-1341's blood result is therefore a small underpowered subset of P-1275's pool, not a separate body of evidence that could contradict it.

results.quantity:
The two papers estimate different quantities.
P-249 (Reparaz-Escudero 2024): the SMD (random effects with HKSJ adjustment) of change in global cognitive function, measured from baseline to end of study. The contrast is 12-month exercise alone against sham physical activity, stretching or social-activity controls. The pool is 3 RCTs (van Uffelen 2008; Lam 2012 and Lam 2015, both cluster RCTs) of community-dwelling older adults with MCI at baseline, including amnestic-MCI/CDR 0.5 participants. Outcomes were MMSE, ADAS-Cog and CDR-SoB.
P-680 (Akalp 2024): a standardised difference in means, standardised by the SD of change scores, of one composite per study that combines every cognitive outcome across all domains (TMT, digit span, logical memory, verbal fluency, MMSE, MoCA). It is measured at the end of mostly 6-28-week programmes, with one 101-week trial. The contrast is exercise against a no-exercise condition. The pool is controlled trials, not restricted to RCTs, of MCI with no stated subtype; the amnestic-MCI trials were removed. It rests on 20 effect-size entries from 18 studies.
results.finding_a: P-249, section 3.10, p.12. Long-term exercise had "a negligible impact on participants diagnosed with MCI at baseline (SMD = 0.06; 95 %CI: -0.10, 0.21)", k=3 (van Uffelen 2008; Lam 2012, 2015; p.13). Exercise alone in all non-demented adults: SMD 0.05 (95% CI -0.04 to 0.13), p=0.25, k=9 (p.1 and p.11). All three MCI trials ran 12 months (Table 1, pp.5-6). Their controls were sham physical activity (van Uffelen), sham stretching (Lam 2012) and social activities (Lam 2015) (p.4, Table 1).
results.finding_b: P-680 abstract, p.1, and section 3.3, p.5. Exercise against control on cognition: ES 1.165 (95% CI 0.741 to 1.589), Z=5.389, p<0.001. Heterogeneity: Q=158.930 on df=19, I2 88.0%, tau2 0.782. Prediction interval -0.747 to 3.077. The 4 amnestic-MCI trials (259 participants) were not included in the quantitative analysis (p.5). The effect is standardised by change-score SD (p.3). Multiple outcomes per study were combined into one effect size (p.3), described as "composite cognitive scores which combined scores from all cognitive domains" (p.15). Durations of the pooled non-amnestic studies (Table 2, pp.6-8) run from 6 weeks (Amjad 2019) to 28 weeks (Chupel 2017), plus one 101-week trial (Molina-Sotomayor 2020). The only 12-month trials, Thomas 2020 and Stuckenschneider 2021, were amnestic and excluded; Stuckenschneider found "Composite Cognition ↔".
results.same_quantity:
No. Element by element:
(1) Intervention class: roughly matched. Both pool exercise alone without a cognitive task; P-249's MCI trials are walking, tai chi and a qigong/aerobic multicomponent.
(2) Comparator: differs. P-249's three MCI trials all used attention-matched sham, stretching or social-activity controls, and P-249 says the active controls "partially diluted the observed effects" (pp.14-15). P-680 excluded studies without a no-exercise condition (p.3).
(3) Outcome construct: differs. P-249 uses global screening or staging instruments (MMSE, ADAS-Cog, CDR-SoB). P-680 pools a per-study composite of all domain-specific tests, which it lists as a limitation (p.15).
(4) Horizon: differs. P-249 measures at 12 months. In P-680, 18 of the 19 non-amnestic studies ran 6-28 weeks (median about 12-16 weeks); only Molina-Sotomayor reached 101 weeks.
(5) Population subtype: differs. P-249's Lam 2012 enrolled CDR 0.5 or amnestic-MCI participants, and van Uffelen and Lam 2015 enrolled Petersen/IWG MCI. P-680 removed all amnestic-labelled trials, so what remains has no stated subtype.
(6) Design: P-249 includes RCTs only, with cluster adjustment. P-680 admits any design with a control group and used a quality checklist built for randomised and non-randomised designs (p.3).
(7) Metric: both are SMD-type change contrasts. P-680 states that it standardises by change-score SD with a pre-post correlation. P-249 does not state its standardiser, so the scaling may also differ.
Four of the rule's same-quantity elements (comparison, outcome, horizon, population class) differ. This matches the precedents C-227 (different comparators) and C-234 (different instruments pooled).
results.incompatible:
Taken as numbers alone, the 95% CIs are disjoint: P-249's upper bound of 0.21 is below P-680's lower bound of 0.741. If the two estimated the same quantity, both could not be true, and this is not a significance-only difference. But the estimands differ in comparator (sham/active vs no exercise), outcome (global instrument vs all-domain composite), horizon (12 months vs about 3-6 months) and subtype. The disjoint intervals are therefore two different quantities, not a contradiction about one. Two points in the source documents fit the moderator reading:
- P-680's prediction interval (-0.747 to 3.077) contains P-249's 0.06.
- P-680's own 12-month trial (Stuckenschneider 2021, amnestic MCI, 118 participants, composite cognition unchanged) was excluded from its pool, and its null matches P-249.

results.quantity: Each side measures something different. P-517 (ALE meta-analysis): how closely the published peak foci for "increased ALFF/fALFF, MCI > HC" cluster in space. The foci were pooled from 4 experiments, and the right-hemisphere cluster peaks in the right fusiform gyrus, BA37, at MNI (51,-60,-12), cluster 12,656 mm3, with a second peak in the right declive at (39,-69,-9). P-529 (single-site primary study): a voxelwise two-sample t-test of mean-standardised ALFF (global signal regressed) in 30 MCI vs 30 HC. The decreased cluster peaks in the right inferior temporal gyrus, labelled BA20 by the authors, at MNI (60,-45,-12), 107 voxels (about 2,889 mm3 at 3 mm isotropic), T = -3.68, FDR p<0.05. The two peaks are 17.5 mm apart (dx 9, dy 15, dz 0), and P-529's peak is 32 mm from P-517's second peak. Neither paper shows any shared voxel.
results.finding_a: P-517 (Yuan et al. 2021, Front Aging Neurosci), p.4: "Compared to HC, MCI patients demonstrated increased ALFF/fALFF in the bilateral cerebellum posterior lobe, right parahippocampal gyrus and bilateral fusiform gyrus". The analysis is "increased ALFF/fALFF (n = 75; foci14)" (p.4). Table 2 (p.7) gives cluster 5: 12,656 mm3, peak (51,-60,-12), right fusiform gyrus, BA37, max ALE 0.00765; sub-peak (39,-69,-9), right declive, ALE 0.00719. By Table 1 (p.6), only 4 of the 5 ALFF/fALFF studies contribute MCI>HC foci: Yin 2014 (2), Wang 2011 (8), Cai 2015 (2), Jing 2012 (4). Zhao 2015 contributes 0. That totals 16 foci, not 14, from about 76 MCI patients. The paper reports no ALE threshold, no p-value and no correction method anywhere. It also says the fusiform change was the smallest ALFF change: "the smallest change occurred in the fusiform gyrus" (p.4). ALFF and fALFF foci are pooled together. Studies were selected on "an analysis of DMN in the resting state".
results.finding_b: P-529 (Lai et al. 2022, Front Mol Neurosci), baseline cross-sectional contrast before moxibustion. Methods (p.3): two-sample t-test on normalised ALFF, voxel-level FDR p<0.05, global signal regressed. Sample (p.4): 30 MCI vs 30 HC, age 55-75, CDR 0.5, memory complaint. Table 3 (p.5): decreased in MCI at R_ITG, BA20, peak (60,-45,-12), 107 voxels, T = -3.68. Also decreased at R_TPOmid (27,5,-36) and L_MCC (-12,-36,45). Increased in MCI at L_HIPP (-24,-39,3), L_MTG (-54,-45,12), R_LING (9,-69,-3) and R_MOG (27,-72,24). No right-fusiform change is reported at baseline.
results.same_quantity:
No, on several elements.
(1) Location: the candidate's "at matching voxels" is not supported by the source tables. P-517's peak is in the right fusiform gyrus (BA37, 51,-60,-12). P-529's peak is in the right lateral inferior temporal gyrus (BA20, 60,-45,-12), 17.5 mm anterolateral. P-517's cluster runs posteromedially toward its second peak (39,-69,-9), away from P-529's peak. As a sphere, its volume would have a radius of about 14.5 mm, and its likely centroid is about 24 mm from P-529's peak. Neither figure shows overlap: P-517 Fig. 2 is a surface projection and P-529 Fig. 1 shows single slices. The ALE cluster extent comes mostly from the smoothing kernel, so it does not show where ALFF was actually observed to rise.
(2) Estimand type: an ALE map says how likely reported foci are to converge. It is not a pooled effect estimate at a voxel. P-529 reports a voxelwise t-statistic from one sample.
(3) Measure: P-517 pools ALFF with fALFF, a different ratio metric. P-529 uses mean-standardised ALFF after global signal regression.
(4) Population: comparable. P-517's includes are amnestic MCI in older adults (Table 2 footnote). P-529 is memory-complaint MCI, CDR 0.5, aged 55-75.
(5) Contrast: comparable, both cross-sectional MCI vs HC.
results.incompatible:
No. Both results can hold at once: ALFF can be raised in the right posterior fusiform gyrus and lowered in the adjacent lateral inferior temporal gyrus. This is a claim about region X against a claim about region Y, which the rule lists as not incompatible.
Two further problems apply even if the edges of the clusters overlapped:
(a) P-517's "increase" has no inferential statistic in the paper. There is no threshold, p-value or correction, and Table 2 has internal anomalies: the left fusiform cluster's max ALE is printed as 0, and the largest increase cluster, the paracentral lobule at 19,336 mm3, has max ALE 0.0019. With 4 experiments and 14-16 foci, the convergence could come from a single study's focus.
(b) An ALE convergence does not assert an increase at every voxel of the cluster, so a nearby FDR-significant decrease in one sample cannot contradict it.
If the location mismatch were set aside, the ALE-vs-t-test difference would still make this documented incommensurability, not a contradiction.

results.quantity: The two sides measure different things. P-517 (Yuan et al. 2021, ALE meta-analysis): where in the brain the reported peak coordinates of between-group FC differences cluster (MCI>HC and MCI<HC) across 27 rs-fMRI FC studies. The seeds and methods of those studies differ and are not stated. The output is a map of locations with ALE values, not a connectivity estimate for any seed-target pair. P-774 (Guan et al. 2022): the strength of FC from a PCC seed (MNI -5,-49,40, 10 mm sphere) to the bilateral medial superior frontal gyrus and to the bilateral middle cingulate gyrus, clinical aMCI (n=40) vs HC (n=38), ANCOVA adjusted for age, sex and education.
results.finding_a: P-517, p.4 and Table 2 (p.7). In MCI vs HC, FC-increase foci (n=604; 85 foci from 17 studies) cluster in one 848 mm3 cluster. It has two peaks, both in ventral BA10: right medial frontal gyrus at MNI (4, 58, -14), ALE 0.0156, and left anterior cingulate at (-6, 56, -12), ALE 0.0126. The prose calls these 'right medial frontal gyrus, left limbic lobe and left ACC'. FC-decrease foci (n=388; 169 foci) cluster in a 9,168 mm3 precuneus cluster. Its 'Cingulate Gyrus' sub-peak lies in right BA31 at (10, -42, 48), ALE 0.0071, which is posterior cingulate/precuneus territory. Further decrease clusters are occipital, temporal and angular. No seed is given for any cluster, no study contributions per cluster are given, and there is no effect size or confidence interval for any connectivity value. The authors say their pool mixes studies with different seeds.
results.finding_b: P-774, PDF p.6-7 (journal pp.708-709). 137 analysed: 24 RGD-aMCI, 35 RGD, 40 aMCI and 38 HC, all Han Chinese aged 60-80, from a single centre in Nanjing. PCC-seed FC differed among the four groups (ANCOVA, AlphaSim p<0.01, eta2 0.085-0.141) in bilateral M-SFG, bilateral angular gyrus, bilateral MCG and L-MFG. Post hoc, aMCI vs HC: PCC-to-bilateral-M-SFG FC was significantly reduced (Fig. 2c) and PCC-to-bilateral-MCG FC was significantly increased (Fig. 2c). RGD-aMCI showed decreased MCG FC vs HC. In aMCI, PCC-M-SFG FC correlated with Rey-CFT-DR (r=0.47, p=0.003). No aMCI vs HC result is reported for L-MFG. Peak coordinates and post hoc effect sizes are only in Supplementary Tables S3/S4, which are not in the article PDF.
results.same_quantity: No, element by element. (1) Measure. P-517's FC result is a convergence map of where reported FC-difference peaks fall. A focus at a location means some study found a group FC difference there relative to that study's own seed or network. The authors confirm the pool is not restricted by seed: 'we do not rule out the literature based on seed method ... The different seed selection point will influence results'. Table 1 has no seed column and no contribution list per cluster, so nothing shows the medial frontal cluster came from PCC-seeded experiments. Bai et al. (2009), a PCC-seed study in the pool, contributed 5 increase and 0 decrease foci, but which cluster they fed is not reported. So 'increased FC in medial frontal gyrus' in P-517 is not 'PCC-to-medial-frontal FC is increased'. P-774's quantity is one specific edge from a PCC seed. (2) Region, frontal. P-517's increase peaks sit at z = -12 to -14 in BA10: ventromedial/orbital prefrontal cortex, with pregenual/subgenual ACC. P-774's target is the medial superior frontal gyrus, whose coordinates are not in the article. Overlap is not established, and the labels point to dorsal vs ventral medial PFC. (3) Region, cingulate. P-517's 'cingulate' decrease is a BA31 sub-peak inside the precuneus cluster, about 18 mm from the centre of P-774's PCC seed. That is posterior cingulate/precuneus territory, close to P-774's seed itself. P-774's increase is in the middle cingulate gyrus as target. These are different subregions and different edges. (4) Metric type. P-517 gives an ALE convergence statistic with no effect estimate. P-774 gives a voxelwise Fisher-z FC difference with an F/post hoc test. (5) Population. Both are clinical MCI in older adults: P-517 pools MCI-vs-HC studies and its legends call MCI 'amnestic'; P-774's aMCI group has no depression history and no biomarker confirmation. Population is the only element that roughly matches.
results.incompatible: No. Both results can be true at once. P-517's increase foci in ventral BA10/ACC may come from seeds other than the PCC, such as hippocampal, mPFC or ICA-component analyses. They are in a different medial-frontal subregion from P-774's M-SFG target. A location map pooled across seeds cannot be contradicted by a decrease on one PCC edge. Likewise, P-517's reduced FC in the posterior cingulate/precuneus (BA31) region is compatible with P-774's increased PCC-to-middle-cingulate FC. P-517 also reports no uncertainty that another estimate could fall outside. On the posterior-DMN side the two papers agree: P-517 finds convergent FC decreases centred on the precuneus/PCC, and P-774 finds reduced PCC-seed FC to M-SFG.

results.quantity: The two papers do not report the same quantity. P-644 reports the fully adjusted OR for prevalent MCI per 1 m/s of continuous usual gait speed (Petersen-modified MCI: memory complaint, education-stratified MMSE, CDRS <=0.5, IADL >=6; community adults aged 60+ in Tianjin and Shanghai). P-878 reports the adjusted OR for MCI defined as AACD (>=1 SD below the age norm on a 31-point HRS-style telephone battery; CHARLS 2015, aged 50+, stroke excluded) for a BINARY gait-speed category, not per unit. Its Table 1 gives GS as n (%). On the paper's AWGS 2019 definition (<1.0 m/s over a 2.5 m walk) the category is slow gait. The secondary checks also differ: handgrip is per kg in both papers but the MCI construct differs, and depressive symptoms are a binary GDS-30 >=11 in P-644 against a CESD-10 score per point in P-878.
results.finding_a: P-644 (Chen X et al. 2021, J Affect Disord; n=1394, 241 MCI / 1153 normal), Table 2, PDF page 4, adjusted for 12 covariates. Gait speed OR 0.16 (0.07-0.35), p<0.001; crude 0.05 (0.03-0.10). Handgrip OR 0.97 (0.94-0.99), p=0.006. Depressive symptoms (GDS-30 >=11) OR 1.82 (1.20-2.76), p=0.005. Sarcopenia OR 1.67 (1.04-2.68), p=0.033. SMI 0.86 (0.70-1.08), not significant. Descriptively (Table 1, page 3), gait speed is 0.97+-0.23 m/s in MCI vs 1.11+-0.21 m/s in normal cognition, and handgrip 20.49 vs 24.79 kg. So faster gait and stronger grip go with lower MCI odds.
results.finding_b:
P-878 (Chen L et al. 2024, Heliyon; CHARLS 2015; n=2431, 439 MCI / 1992 normal), Table 2, PDF page 6. GS crude 2.11 (1.477-3.016), adjusted 1.571 (1.076-2.291). HGS crude 1.07 (1.056-1.084), adjusted 1.047 (1.028-1.066). FTSST adjusted 0.946. ASMI adjusted 1.405. Possible sarcopenia crude 0.635, adjusted 0.718 (0.555-0.928). Sarcopenia crude 1.647, adjusted 1.357 (1.031-1.787). Depressive symptom crude 0.940, adjusted 0.956 (0.937-0.976).

Table 1 (page 5) shows these ORs cannot be read at face value:
- GS is reported as a count, 1668 (83.73%) of normal-cognition participants vs 402 (91.57%) of MCI participants. The crude OR recomputed from these counts with MCI as the event is exactly 2.110.
- Possible sarcopenia, 395 (19.83%) vs 123 (28.02%), gives an MCI-event OR of 1.574. Its reciprocal, 0.635, is what the table prints.
- Sarcopenia counts give an MCI-event OR of 1.647, which is what the table prints.
- Every continuous exposure has a crude OR running against its own group difference under MCI-as-event coding: HGS 27.25 in MCI vs 31.83 in normal cognition (OR 1.07), FTSST 9.81 vs 9.02 s (0.918), ASMI 8.58 vs 8.34 (0.845), CESD-10 6 vs 5 (0.940).

The mediation model with MCI as the dependent variable gives a positive depressive-symptom-to-MCI total effect (c = 0.006, P<0.001, page 6). The authors' own text treats every component as a risk association.
results.same_quantity:
No.
- Exposure scale: P-644 uses continuous gait speed per 1 m/s. P-878 uses a binary gait category whose crude OR reproduces exactly from its Table 1 counts, most plausibly slow gait (AWGS 2019, <1.0 m/s, 2.5 m walk, fastest of two trials). P-644 used usual gait speed with AWGS 2014 (<0.8 m/s).
- Outcome construct: P-644 uses clinical-style Petersen-modified MCI (memory complaint, education-stratified MMSE, CDRS, IADL). P-878 uses a psychometric AACD cut-off (>=1 SD below the age norm) on a telephone HRS battery.
- Population: both are Chinese community-dwelling adults, but the age floors are 60 vs 50 and P-878 excluded stroke.
- Adjustment sets differ: P-644 adjusts for nutrition (MNA-SF), sleep and IPAQ; P-878 adjusts for 17 chronic-disease and lifestyle covariates, with BMI in the table footnote.
- Handgrip is per kg in both, the closest element, but the MCI constructs and dynamometer protocols differ (GRIP-D, dominant hand vs WL-1000, maximum of both hands).
- Depressive symptoms: a binary GDS-30 >=11 vs a continuous CESD-10 score per point, so different quantities.
results.incompatible:
No. P-878's own statistics do not support the opposite direction on any of the three exposures, and read against its own data it agrees with P-644.

(1) Gait: P-878's GS crude OR (2.11) is exactly the 2x2 OR, with MCI as the event, for the GS category that is more common in MCI (91.57% vs 83.73%). The paper says the MCI group had 'poorer ... physical performance', and its only gait category is AWGS low physical function (<1.0 m/s). So the finding is 'slow gait raises MCI odds' (adjusted OR 1.571), the same direction as P-644's OR 0.16 per m/s faster.

(2) Handgrip and depressive symptoms: with a single predictor, the sign of the univariable logistic coefficient follows the sign of the case-minus-control mean difference. All four continuous crude ORs in P-878 run opposite to its Table 1 group differences under MCI=1 coding (HGS lower in MCI yet OR 1.07; CESD higher in MCI yet OR 0.940; likewise FTSST and ASMI). So these ORs were estimated with normal cognition as the event, or with reversed sign.

(3) The table mixes direction coding. Possible sarcopenia 0.635 is the exact reciprocal of the MCI-event OR from its counts, while sarcopenia 1.647 is the MCI-event OR. That explains the 'sign inconsistency' the candidate flagged.

The mediation total effect of depressive symptoms on MCI is positive (c = 0.006, P<0.001). Correctly oriented, both studies find slower gait, weaker grip, more depressive symptoms and sarcopenia (1.67 vs 1.357) associated with higher MCI odds. The non-overlapping intervals the candidate cited compare an inverted or binary P-878 estimate with P-644's continuous per-m/s estimate.

results.quantity: Both papers look at how age (per year, at MCI classification) relates to reversion from MCI to normal cognition, but each estimates a different quantity. P-986 reports a fully adjusted Poisson incidence rate ratio (IRR) per year of age for incident reversion, with a person-time offset and robust variance. The contrast is reverters versus stable MCI only, in one Swedish community cohort (Good Aging in Skane, Petersen criteria, n = 744, aged 60 to 102, mean age 68.4). P-711 reports a random-effects pooled mean odds ratio per year of age across 19 heterogeneous studies. Those studies use different countries, settings (community and hospital), diagnostic criteria, follow-up lengths and comparison groups, and the paper does not say whether crude or adjusted ORs were pooled. The pool very probably contains P-986 itself, and also Overton 2019 from the same cohort.
results.finding_a: P-986 (Overton et al. 2023, J Alzheimers Dis 91:585-601). Table 4 (journal p.596, PDF p.12), Petersen-criteria model: age (y) IRR 1.02 (95% CI 1.01 to 1.03), p < 0.001. NP-criteria model (n = 375): IRR 1.00 (0.98 to 1.02), p = 0.885, i.e. null. Average adjusted predicted probability of reversion under Petersen (p.593): 0.38 (0.33 to 0.42) at age 60 against 0.46 (0.42 to 0.50) at age 70. The model adjusts for sex, education, cohabitation, physical activity, alcohol, BMI, cardiovascular disease, smoking, sleep disturbances, number of impaired domains and depression (p.589). The reversion comparison group is stable MCI only (p.588). People who progressed to dementia, stopped meeting the criteria, or were lost to follow-up before a qualifying visit are not in the 323 vs 421 contrast. The authors themselves say the direction goes against most previous work. They attribute it to healthy older adults being more likely to attend follow-up, which over-represents cognitively preserved older participants (p.598).
results.finding_b: P-711 (Zhao et al. 2025, Geriatric Nursing 63:379-387). Table 3 (journal p.384, PDF p.6): Age(y), N = 19 studies, OR 0.94 (0.92 to 0.96), I2 = 92.5%, P < 0.001. Discussion (p.384): 'younger age had a high possibility to recover'. Method (p.380): ORs and 95% CIs were 'extracted from included studies' and pooled with random effects when I2 >= 50%. The paper does not report a prediction interval, a forest plot for age, a list of the 19 age studies, a meta-regression, or a leave-one-out analysis. Table 1 (p.381) lists Overton 2023 (ref 38, DOI 10.3233/jad-220597, which is P-986: Swedish, n = 744, 43.4%, Petersen) with 'age' among its included factors. It also lists Overton 2019 (ref 48, same Good Aging in Skane cohort, n = 331, Mayo criteria) with 'age'. 21 studies in Table 1 list age, and 19 were pooled. The paper's prose has transcription errors: on p.383 the female-sex and BMI results are printed with CIs and I2 copied from the education and age rows (e.g. 'female sex (OR=1.02 95% CI:1.01 to 1.04, I2= 92.5%, P=0.553)', whereas Table 3 gives 0.95 (0.79 to 1.13)). The Table 3 age row agrees with the discussion.
results.same_quantity:
No, element by element.
(1) Estimand type: P-711 estimates the mean of a distribution of setting-specific age effects across 19 heterogeneous studies (I2 92.5%). P-986 estimates the age effect in one setting. The pool very probably includes that setting's own estimate (P-986 is listed in Table 1 with age as an included factor), plus a second estimate from the same cohort (Overton 2019). A pooled mean cannot be set against one of its own inputs as independent, same-quantity evidence.
(2) Metric type: P-986 reports an IRR (reversion rate per person-year, with offset). P-711 reports an OR, and it is not stated how IRRs, HRs or categorical age contrasts from the inputs were converted.
(3) Comparison group: P-986 compares reverters with stable MCI only and drops progressors and people who became ineligible. P-986 itself warns that 'researchers must be mindful of the comparison group' (p.597). P-711 pools studies whose non-reverter groups vary, and many include progressors. Conditioning on staying non-demented and attending follow-up is exactly the selection the P-986 authors blame for their older-age direction.
(4) Adjustment set: P-986 adjusts for 12 covariates. P-711 does not say whether crude or adjusted ORs were pooled, and the inputs' adjustment sets differ.
(5) Population class: both are older adults with clinically classified MCI. P-711 pools community and hospital samples from Asia, Europe, the Americas and Australia under at least six criterion sets. P-986 is a single Swedish community cohort under algorithmic Petersen criteria. The broad population class matches, but together with (1) to (4) the two numbers do not estimate the same thing.
results.incompatible:
Not incompatible in the rule's sense. The candidate says the intervals 'exclude each other' (1.01 to 1.03 against 0.92 to 0.96), but a random-effects CI describes uncertainty about the mean effect, not about any single study's effect. With I2 = 92.5%, the model expects individual studies to lie on both sides of the mean.

P-711 reports no prediction interval, so I made a rough one from its reported summary. Assuming roughly equal weights: SE(log mean) about 0.011, total variance about 19 x SE^2, tau about 0.046, and an approximate 95% prediction interval of about 0.85 to 1.04. That interval contains P-986's 1.02. This is my back-of-envelope estimate, not a figure either paper reports.

On top of that, P-986's estimate is very probably one of the inputs that produced the pooled mean and its heterogeneity, so the two numbers cannot both be treated as independent claims about one quantity. P-986's NP-criteria model on the same cohort is null (1.00, 0.98 to 1.02). P-986's authors name a design-specific mechanism for their direction: selective attendance, with a stable-MCI-only comparison group.

A study-level disagreement does exist: P-986 goes against most earlier single studies, as its own authors say. But this pair (a cohort against a meta-analytic mean that absorbs it) is not a valid test of it. P-217|P-986 is the cleaner pair for that question.

The intervals are disjoint (0.21 < 0.24) and the two studies disagree on significance. Direction is coded the same way in both: positive means the exercise group improved more. In P-674 this shows in Bademli (3.27 vs -1.18, SMD +2.69); P-674's RevMan axis labels are inverted, but the data and text are not.

Gates:
- Task: T6 in both.
- Validation tier: not applicable to syntheses, so matched.
- Modality family: global-cognition screening instruments in both, so matched.
- Dataset family: the trial pools overlap on two trials. A waiver is available: population-level intervention effect, both samples being older community-dwelling adults with clinically diagnosed MCI.

I also tried every subgroup the two papers share:
- Aerobic: P-249 0.10 (-0.10, 0.30) vs P-674 0.79 (0.35, 1.23). Disjoint.
- Resistance: P-249 0.00 (-0.09, 0.08) vs P-674 0.67 (0.22, 1.12). Disjoint.
- Tai chi/neuromotor: 0.11 (-0.06, 0.28) vs 0.57 (-0.06, 1.19). Overlapping.
- Multicomponent: 0.05 (-0.18, 0.17) vs 0.37 (-0.18, 0.92). Overlapping.
- The frequency meta-regression and depression appear in P-674 only. Dementia and MCI incidence and verbal fluency appear in P-249 only.

The disjoint aerobic and resistance pairs fail on population. P-249's aerobic arms are van Uffelen (MCI) plus Muscari, Zotcheva and Komulainen, all cognitively healthy. Its resistance arms (Bischoff-Ferrari, Komulainen) are cognitively healthy only. P-674 is MCI only.

- Lam 2015: -0.04 [-0.28, 0.19]

- Lam 2012: 0.11 [-0.14, 0.36]
- Lam 2015: 0.11 [-0.13, 0.35]
- MCI pool: 0.06 [-0.10, 0.21]

The strongest case for a genuine contradiction is the male stratum. The quantity would be the adjusted hazard ratio for incident all-cause dementia (ICD-coded) comparing obese with non-obese older US adults (aged 50 or over) who have ICD-coded MCI, in men.

The model adjusts for age, sex, race, ethnicity, cerebrovascular disease, stroke, MI, hypertension, diabetes, alcohol abuse and sleep apnea. The female HR is 0.99, so sex does not shift the baseline hazard.

Matching is 1:1 propensity score on age, sex, race, diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, cerebrovascular disease, alcohol and others.

- Both are US EHR samples of adults aged 50 or over with ICD-coded MCI.
- Both exclude people with prior dementia.
- Both use ICD-coded all-cause dementia as the outcome.
- Both estimate a confounder-adjusted HR, with overlapping adjustment sets that include the obesity mediators diabetes and hypertension.

- **Reference group.** Recombining P-1081's reference from normal to non-obese (normal, overweight and underweight weighted by their training-set counts) moves the obese HR only to about 0.82, and its interval still excludes P-1151's 0.97-1.13 overall and 1.01-1.26 in men.
- **Sex.** P-1151's male stratum removes the sex-mix objection (96% vs 45% male).
- **Horizon.** Horizon does not rescue P-1081's 0.75. In P-1151's obesity Kaplan-Meier panel the two curves are visibly superimposed through about year 4-5, so over P-1081's 5-year window P-1151 shows no protective separation. This is a visual reading, not a reported estimate.

The gates can plausibly be met:
- **Task.** T2 vs T4, but both are association HRs, so the mismatch could be waived.
- **Dataset family.** Waivable: this is a population-level association, and both samples are US EHR adults aged 50 or over with ICD-coded clinical MCI.
- **Validation tier.** Not applicable to an association, so it counts as matched.
- **Modality family.** EHR/clinical in both.

On the numbers alone, then, the directions are opposite and the intervals are disjoint. The advocate case fails on one element: the exposure definition.

VERDICT: documented_incommensurability (confidence: moderate-high). Applied as written, the rule does not make this pair genuine.

WHY THE STRONGEST CASE FAILS

(1) The rule requires opposite directions "each supported by the study's own statistics". P-671's only reported adjusted age estimate compares reverters with CONVERTERS: 0.79, with 0.88 for maintainers versus converters. The reverters-versus-staying-MCI figure (about 0.90) is my derivation; P-671 does not report it. P-671's own statistic on that contrast is the unadjusted post hoc test (R 69.6 < M 72.3, p.4). P-986's unadjusted equivalent points the same way or shows no difference:
- Petersen: 68.2 v 68.5
- NP: 66.8 v 69.3 (reverters younger)
So on each paper's own statistics for the shared contrast, the two agree. The opposite direction appears only when P-671's reported estimate (versus converters) is set against P-986's (versus stable MCI), and those are different comparisons.

(2) Metric type and horizon differ. P-671 gives odds of the state at a single reassessment after 4 years. P-986 gives a first-reversion rate over a median of 7.0 years of person-time, with an offset from the first MCI visit to reversion or end of follow-up. For the age covariate the difference changes the estimate, not just the scale. P-986's visit interval is 3 years for people over 78 and 6 years for those under 78 (journal p.587). Older participants therefore have more chances to be detected as reverted, and shorter time to detection. The rate denominator depends on age by design. The AAP probabilities come out of that same rate model.

(3) Outcome definitions differ:
- P-986 counts a reversion only when the complaint is retained, ADL is intact and dementia is absent (p.588). It drops people who stop meeting MCI criteria: 35.9% of MCI cases under Petersen (p.599).
- P-671 codes normal cognition by NCGG-FAT, with converters defined by MMSE<24 or dementia, and has no complaint requirement. 325 of its 769 outcomes are imputed by multivariate normal imputation from first-wave covariates, age among them (p.2). Only about 24 of the 256 reverters come from imputed records: 232 of 444 reverted in the observed data (p.4).

(4) P-986's own authors attribute the positive age association to selective attendance by cognitively preserved older adults (journal p.598). The association also disappears in the same cohort under the NP criteria: 1.00 (0.98-1.02), p=0.885. This does not by itself dissolve a contradiction, but it confirms that P-986's age estimate depends on the design and case definition rather than measuring the quantity P-671 reports. This matches the precedents: different contrasts or estimands give documented incommensurability, as in C-204 and C-227.

GATES
- Task: T5 in both; matched.
- Dataset family: NCGG-SGS (Obu, Japan, 65+) versus GAS/SNAC (Skane, Sweden, 60+). Mismatched. A waiver on population grounds would be available (a population-level association; community-dwelling older adults with MCI), but it is moot because same-quantity fails.
- Validation tier: V2 in both rows, not applicable to association studies; counted as matched.
- Modality family: demographic exposure with a neuropsychological outcome in both; matched. The registry subtypes differ.

INDEPENDENCE: Distinct cohorts and distinct author groups (NCGG versus Lund); independent.

RECORD OF ERRORS
- The candidate's quantity says "reversion vs non-reversion", but P-671's reported estimate is reversion versus conversion (converters are the reference).
- P-671 Table 5 is internally inconsistent: walking speed OR 6.89 (1.87-25.30) is labelled p>0.05. This lowers confidence in that table.
- P-986's text points to Table 3 for the Poisson factors; the factors are in Table 4.
- P-986's Discussion gives 42.4% where the Results give 43.4%.

WHAT WOULD CHANGE THE VERDICT
The verdict would move toward genuine if both of the following were reported:
- P-671 with maintainers as the reference category (reverters versus maintainers, adjusted, in the observed 444 without imputation)
- P-986 as a cumulative odds or fixed-horizon estimate for reversion versus stable MCI, with the age-dependent visit schedule handled (for example, restricted to under-78s or at a fixed 6-year assessment)
If both then showed opposite directions with intervals excluding 1, the pair would be genuine.
